An estimated 20-30 hours will be dedicated to the research and preparation of the Data Management Plan (DMP). This includes the time required to identify and describe the dataset, ensure adherence to FAIR principles, address ethical and legal considerations, and align the plan with institutional guidelines and H2020 mandates. Additionally, time is allocated for reviewing best practices for data sharing, storage, and long-term preservation.
Significant computational time is required: the current extraction pipeline has a runtime of approximately 40 hours. While this is not direct labor time, it represents a substantial computational resource commitment to data retrieval and pre-processing.

For the AMS Acta data extraction, data management efforts primarily involved time-based resources rather than direct financial costs. The process included developing and executing Python scripts to harvest metadata via the OAI-PMH protocol using the Sickle library, followed by enrichment through JSON exports and implementation of custom filtering logic to ensure institutional relevance. Ensuring that the resulting dataset adhered to FAIR principles - particularly Findability and Reusability - required structured storage, documentation of the filtering criteria, and clear mapping to persistent identifiers (ePrint IDs and ORCIDs). While no dedicated budget was allocated, the data management tasks were integrated into the overall project timeline and conducted by team members with technical expertise in metadata handling and research data management.
The data is openly available on Zenodo.

data_quality_assurance:
To ensure the consistency and quality of the research output, the following
measures were implemented throughout the project:
Standardized Data Capture: Data was harvested using well-established protocols
(e.g., OAI-PMH) and APIs, ensuring consistent metadata formats and reducing
errors introduced by manual collection.
Data Validation and Cleaning: Automated scripts include validation checks to
detect incomplete, empty, or malformed metadata records, filtering out unreliable
or irrelevant entries. Affiliation and ORCID filters ensure only relevant records are
retained.
Use of Controlled Vocabularies and Identifiers: Where applicable, standard
identifiers such as ORCID for authors and repository-specific persistent identifiers
for research outputs were used to maintain uniformity and improve data linking.
Documentation of Processing Steps: Every stage of data collection, cleaning,
filtering, and merging is scripted and documented, facilitating reproducibility and
transparency.
Peer Review and Cross-Verification: The collected and processed data were crossverified against multiple repositories to identify overlaps, discrepancies, and
coverage gaps, which helps highlight potential inconsistencies.
Iterative Testing and Calibration: Scripts and workflows were tested iteratively on
subsets of data to fine-tune parameters and confirm robustness before scaling to
the full dataset.
Version Control and Change Tracking: All code and data processing steps are
maintained under version control (GitHub), allowing tracking of changes and
reverting to previous states if issues are detected.
dataset.description: The research relies on a set of Python scripts and open-source libraries developed to collect, merge, and analyze data from multiple institutional and external repositories. Key data sources include AMS Acta (UNIBO’s institutional open access repository for long-term preservation of scientific outputs), Software Heritage (the largest public archive of source code and development history), Zenodo (an interdisciplinary platform by CERN for secure data preservation), IRIS (UNIBO’s Current Research Information System for institutional research traceability), and OpenCitations (a platform for citation data and scholarly network analysis). Custom scripts were written to harvest metadata and content from these repositories, clean and merge datasets, and perform quantitative analyses addressing the main research questions: (1) the current coverage of diverse UNIBO research outputs across repositories; (2) the extent of overlap among repositories in terms of deposited research objects; (3) citation counts and networks derived from OpenCitations; and (4) mapping and recording of research outputs within IRIS. Visualization scripts complement the analyses by presenting insights clearly. All software and scripts are version-controlled via GitHub, facilitating reproducibility, collaboration, and transparent open science practices.
dataset.preservation_statement: The code is uploaded on GitHub and available on Zenodo for easy replicability.

data_quality_assurance:
To ensure the quality and consistency of the research output, the following measures will be implemented:

  • Standardized Data Capture: Data collection will adhere to internationally recognized standards (e.g., Dublin Core, PROV-O) to ensure uniformity and consistency across datasets.
  • Data Entry Validation: Automated validation checks will be employed to ensure that the data entered into the system is accurate and free from errors. This includes checks for missing or inconsistent data points.
  • Peer Review: The dataset and any associated software will undergo internal review by project team members and external experts to ensure its validity and usability.
  • Controlled Vocabularies: Controlled vocabularies and standardized terminologies (e.g., DCMI, Creative Commons licenses) will be used to ensure uniform data representation and facilitate its reuse.

dataset.preservation_statement:
For the purposes of this project, we plan to preserve the metadata extracted from Software Heritage, along with any processed or derived datasets, such as merged data from multiple repositories (e.g., Zenodo, AMS Acta) and the software developed for analysis. The datasets will be stored in a trusted, open-access repository, such as Zenodo, which supports long-term preservation and is designed specifically for this type of research output.

We carefully evaluated the data to ensure that only relevant and necessary information is preserved for long-term access. For example, large datasets or files that do not directly contribute to the project's goals (e.g., intermediate raw data) are excluded from long-term storage to minimize the size and complexity of the preserved data.

In the case of software or tools developed as part of the project, we retain the final versions of these outputs, ensuring that they are documented and properly licensed for reuse. The decision of what to preserve are based on the relevance of the data and software to the project's goals, as well as their future utility for researchers and practitioners.

dataset.preservation_statement:
At this stage, no data is subject to contractual or legal retention or destruction obligations. However, a selection process for long-term preservation may be implemented to retain only the filtered and cleaned metadata records relevant to
researchers affiliated with the University of Bologna. The full raw dataset may be discarded after verification, as it is replicable through public APIs (OAI-PMH and AMS Acta JSON export). Preserving only the filtered subset ensures manageable data size and sustained relevance, while respecting data minimization and reproducibility principles.

dmp.description:
This Data Management Plan (DMP) supports the final project for the Open Science course, taught by Professor Silvio Peroni within the Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge master’s programme at the University of Bologna during the 2024/2025 academic year.

The project investigates how diverse research outputs - such as software, databases, exhibitions, and audiovisual materials - produced by researchers and personnel at the University of Bologna (UNIBO) are represented and disseminated across various repositories. 

The team gathers metadata from institutional, disciplinary, and generalist repositories - including AMS Acta, Software Heritage, and Zenodo - using APIs and metadata dumps. It examines cross-repository depositions and overlaps, analyzes citation dynamics, and evaluates the extent to which these outputs are integrated into UNIBO’s Current Research Information System (IRIS).

The project addresses the following research questions:
  • RQ1: What is the current coverage of these types of research outputs created by UNIBO personnel in institutional, disciplinary, and generalist repositories?
  • RQ2: To what extent is there overlap among these repositories (i.e., are the same research objects deposited in more than one)?
  • RQ3: How many citations (incoming and outgoing), as recorded in OpenCitations, are associated with these research outputs?
  • RQ4: To what extent are these outputs represented in IRIS?
